3_iteration_stall_recovery.mechanism: _run_phase() bounds each phase to a small max_iterations (default 6, vs the historical 18-iteration monolith) and, on a retryable outcome (iteration_ceiling_reached/timeout/model_unavailable/error -- never on finish/escalate), fails over to the next REAL installed model (_filter_actually_installed(), same real-time check as the whole-job path) rather than blindly re-prompting the same model.
3_iteration_stall_recovery.live_evidence_and_honest_finding: The complexity-class canary (see below) showed something worth being precise about: all 3 base phases were RECORDED as 'error' (their last-attempted-model's outcome), yet real, correct, passing code existed -- file mtimes confirm it was written during the implement/test phase windows. This means an EARLIER model in that phase's failover chain actually completed the work but never cleanly called finish (likely hit iteration_ceiling_reached, which is retryable), so _run_phase correctly tried the NEXT model -- which then failed immediately, and that LAST failure is what got recorded as the phase's outcome, understating the real progress already durably saved in the shared sandbox. This is a genuine, disclosed observability gap (phase records can undersell real progress), not a correctness gap -- because:

7_validation_first_finalization.note: The finding above is exactly why this principle exists and works: job success was decided ENTIRELY by the deterministic validation.validate() (+ canary + independent_validation, identical pipeline to submit_job()) reading the real sandbox state -- NOT by trusting any phase's own self-reported final_action. Even with every phase self-reporting 'error', validation correctly found real, working, passing code and the job correctly finished status=succeeded, promotion_eligible=True. Model says done != job succeeded, proven in both directions this pass: a clean 'finish' claim is still gated behind real validation (implemented previously), and a discouraging 'error' self-report does not block a real success either.
